In reasoning model development, it's always been this interesting tension between training/optimizing chain-of-thoughts (CoTs) vs not touching them to preserve monitorability. CoTs are cool because we can check what the model is up to (e.g., whether it cheats or not) as long as it spells out its thought process. And we risk losing that if we explicitly optimize CoTs. Two caveats: 1) I.e., the catch of CoT and monitorability is that this only works if the written thinking reflects what the model is actually doing. 2) Also, when models become more capable, they spell out less in the CoT (like a cleverer math student needs less note-taking when solving problems during an exam). Nothing new on that front, but an interesting thread below on how to measure "harder to monitor", with some interesting results that confirm the existing intuitions: 1) no-CoT capability (meaning how much reasoning the model can do in a single forward pass without writing anything down) - Better pretraining (lower perplexity) raises this no-CoT capability - Architecture mostly doesn't matter 2) CoT controllability (meaning how well the model can change its written reasoning when asked to add, remove, or change parts of it) - RL alone raises controllability a lot - Controllability is passed on through distillation * Higher no-CoT capability and higher controllability both make monitoring harder. PS: Perhaps the good news is that it seems that process supervision wasn't the main culprit. (1/10) Today, we’re sharing new research from @OpenAI: How does CoT monitorability (no-CoT capability and CoT controllability) evolve over the model training lifecycle? Super interesting work on agent memory. (this is a must-read) It discusses whether agents can manage their own memory. If so, what would that self-organized memory look like? This is the closest implementation that I have seen to my own memory system. I mostly use linked documents with my agents, and it has been working extremely well. It works well because frontier models have gotten better at persisting external knowledge. The problem: Memory systems usually fix the schema in advance, with set record types and rules for how to group them. The solution: SoMem gives the agent ordinary linked documents instead. The agent decides what to summarize, which topics to create, and when to revise them. Every summary links back to the original interaction as evidence, and the runtime builds time, relation, and recency views on top. At question time, the agent chooses what to search and follows links to the source when it needs to check. SoMem beat the strongest baseline by 2.66 points on LoCoMo, 3.10 on BEAM-100K, and 2.00 on LongMemEval-S. Memory built by one model also worked when read by another. If your agent already reads and writes files, try letting it organize memory as linked notes before adding a vector store. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11929 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/can-llm-agents-organize-their-own-memory-2611.11929
